abstract: The circle can be cut into four quadrants, each placed with their origin on the vertices of a square.

In this layout the arcs of the quadrants of an inscribed circle would meet at the midpoints of the sides of the square, leaving some of the square uncovered; the arcs of the quadrants of a circumscribed circle would overlap, and intersect at the center of the square, covering it all.
The arcs of the quadrants of the circle that equals in area to the square intersect right in between those limits, at the quarters on its centerlines.

about.name: Frustum volume

step.description: Express heights via linear proportionality. In similar 3D shapes, linear dimensions scale with the square root of their cross-sectional areas
Because frustum height = pyramid height - tip height, we express both heights in terms of the known frustum height
To eliminate the fraction in the denominator, multiply both the numerator and denominator by base area^(1/2)

step.description: Cancel out the common base area^(1/2) term in the numerator and denominator

about.value: height × top area^(1/2) / (base area^(1/2) - top area^(1/2))

step.description: Substitute the heights into the original equation
Factor out height

Apply the Algebraic Identity (a³ - b³). Let a = √base area and b = √top area . Notice that a³ = √base area × base area and b³ = √top area × top area. The term inside the parentheses is the algebraic quotient
Using the standard difference of cubes factorization
Convert back to area terms

item.name: Area of a Circle = 3.2 × radius²
item.description: The area of a circle is defined by comparing it to a square since that is the base of area calculation. The circle can be cut into four quadrants, each placed with their origin on the vertices of a square. In this layout the arcs of the quadrants of an inscribed circle would meet at the midpoints of the sides of the square, leaving some of the square uncovered. The arcs of the quadrants of a circumscribed circle would overlap, and intersect at the center of the square, covering it all. The arcs of the quadrants of the circle that equals in area to the square intersect right in between those limits, at the quarters on its centerlines. The length of the centerline equals the side length of the square. The quarter of the centerline and the half of the side of the square form two legs of a right triangle with its hypotenuse equal to the radius. The ratio between the radius and the side length is calculable. radius²=(side/2)²+side² radius=side√5/4
item.disambiguatingDescription: The widely used formula  A = pi × r²  is not a result of direct geometric comparison, nor a direct result of calculus. It’s multiplying the approximate circumference formula C = 2pi × r by half the radius, treating the area as the sum of infinitesimal rings. While that method is algebraically valid, it relies on the approximate circumference and bypasses the geometric logic that defines area: the comparison to a square.

item.name: Circumference = 6.4 × radius
item.description: The circumference of a circle is derived from its area algebraically by subtracting a smaller circle and dividing the difference by the difference of the radii. Let x represent the theoretical width of the circumference, which distinguishes it from the rest of the circle. The difference between the shape of the straightened circumference and a quadrilateral is negligible. The length of the two shorter sides of the quadrilateral is x. The length of the two longer sides is the area of the resulting ring divided by x. C=( 3.2 × radius² - 3.2 × ( radius - x )² ) / x   The length of the circumference approaches 6.4 × radius as its thickness approaches 0.
item.disambiguatingDescription: The widely used pi≈3.14... is an artifact of a fundamentally flawed theoretical approximate. It was approximated by assuming that the circumference rests in between the theoretical maximum perimeter of the inscribed polygon and the minimum of the circumscribed polygon.

item.name: Volume of a Sphere = ( √(3.2) × radius )³
item.description: The volume of a sphere is defined by comparing it to a cube, since that is the base of volume calculation. The volume of a sphere equals the cubic value of the square root of its cross-sectional area, just like a cube.
item.disambiguatingDescription: The widely used formula V = 4 / 3 × pi × radius³ was approximated by comparing a hemisphere to the difference between the approximate volume a cone and a circumscribed cylinder. That is a very exaggerated, distortion-based comparison that discards the difference between the straight slant height of a cone and the curvature of a sphere, resulting in a very rough underestimate.

item.name: Volume of a Cone = 3.2 × radius² × height / √8
item.description: The volume of a cone can be calculated by algebraically comparing the volume of a vertical quadrant of a cone with equal radius and height to an octant sphere with equal radius, through a quadrant cylinder. In general: The volume of a cone equals the quarter of a cylinder with an equal radius and its height equal to the height of the cone multiplied by √2.
item.disambiguatingDescription: The volume of a cone is conventionally approximated as base × height / 3. While that is a reasonable rounding, the exact ratio is 1 / √8. The 1 / 3 coefficient was likely estimated based on two observations: 1.:It can be calculated as a pyramid with a polygonal base, and the volume of a pyramid was believed to be base × height / 3, based on the cube dissection method. 2.:The mid-height cross-sectional area of a cone is exactly a quarter of a circumscribed cylinder's with the same base and height. That makes the ratio between the mid-height cross-sectional area of the cone, and the difference between the mid-height cross-sectional areas of the circumscribed cylinder and the cone 1 : 3 .

item.name: Refute of the mathematical constant pi≈3.14...
item.description: The mathematical constant pi≈3.14... was approximated by assuming that the circumference rests in between the theoretical maximum perimeter of the inscribed polygon and the minimum of the circumscribed polygon.
item.disambiguatingDescription: A polygon is called circumscribed if each side is tangent to the circle, meaning that it touches the circle only at exactly one point. Traditional geometry assumes that a tangent line to the circle can always be drawn. When the points adjacent to the tangent point must not coincide with the arc, it implicitly means spatial separation. To maintain a full point of separation over a 3‑point long segment, the sagitta‑to‑chord ratio would need to exceed 3 : 4. Classical tangency is not physically or logically realizable under its own axioms. Without that, the classical argument that the polygons remain tangent indefinitely fails. When the perimeter of a regular polygon equals — or is close enough to — the circumference, the sides are too short to remain tangent to the circle. They cut through the arc. Whether a polygon can be circumscribed about a circle depends on whether its perimeter is sufficiently greater than the circumference. But the bisection procedure guarantees that each new perimeter created by repeatedly bisecting a circumscribed hexagon is smaller than the previous one. The floor of Archimedes’ “upper limit” approaches the ceiling of the lower limit by passing through the true circumference.

item.name: Refute of the traditional Volume of a pyramid = base × height / 3 formula
item.description: The volume of a pyramid is conventionally approximated as base × height / 3. While that is a reasonable rounding, the exact ratio is 1 / √8. A common method aiming to prove the formula V = base × height / 3 involves dissecting a cube into three pyramids.
item.disambiguatingDescription: The cube has 8 vertices, each pyramid has 5. Three pyramids have 3 × 5 = 15 in total. Each vertex of a real physical cube is a point that can't be split into 3 points without duplicating. The other way around, 3 vertices of the pyramids can't be merged into 1 without distortion. If we dissect the cube, we need to designate each shared vertex to be a part of either one pyramid, or another. The volume of each pyramid is exactly a third of the cube, but with a height shorter than the cube's edge, or base smaller than its square value.
